targetQuery: property-based testing C# tutorial / QuickCheck-style generators and shrinking / FsCheck vs CsCheck
comparedAgainst: https://github.com/fscheck/FsCheck (raw README fetched directly) — 'FsCheck is a tool for testing .NET programs automatically.' matches the article's quoted fragment verbatim. Most public FsCheck/PBT tutorials stop at 'here is the API'; this article instead builds a working generator+shrinker from scratch and only reaches for FsCheck/CsCheck at the end, which is a stronger pedagogical structure than the source material itself offers.

https://fscheck.github.io/FsCheck/ (raw HTML fetched and stripped of markup directly, not just a summarized read) — 'When a property fails, FsCheck automatically displays a minimal counter example.' confirmed present verbatim except that the live page spells it as two words, 'counter example', while the article quotes 'counter-example' with a hyphen (see issues; the hyphenated form does appear on the GitHub README the article cites for its other FsCheck quote, so the words and meaning are right, the exact spelling on the specific cited page is not).

https://github.com/AnthonyLloyd/CsCheck (raw README fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com) — 'Gen classes are composable with no need for Arb classes. So less boilerplate.' matches verbatim, character for character, including the two-sentence structure.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.icomparable.compareto — fetched in full. The table cells 'Less than zero' / 'Zero' / 'Greater than zero' that the article quotes match verbatim.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators — fetched in full. 'In an unchecked context, the result is truncated by discarding any high-order bits that don't fit in the destination type.' matches verbatim. 'By default, arithmetic operations occur in an unchecked context' matches verbatim except the article lowercases the initial 'By' to fit mid-sentence, which is normal, non-deceptive quotation practice, not a content change.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.array.sort — fetched in full. Confirms the introsort algorithm: 'If the partition size is less than or equal to 16 elements, it uses an insertion sort algorithm.' The article's paraphrase ('for 16 elements or fewer... Array.Sort runs an insertion sort internally... the comparer runs exactly as written, on exactly the two values given, with nothing skipped') is an accurate, correctly-scoped characterization of that documented behavior, not a quote, so no verbatim obligation applies.

General PBT literature comparison: the large majority of C#/.NET property-based-testing writeups (including FsCheck's and CsCheck's own docs) either show only toy string/int examples or jump straight to library API without ever building a generator or shrinker by hand. This article's decision to hand-roll both, find a genuine bug with them, cross-validate the same bug with CsCheck's real (differently-shaped) shrinker, and only then introduce the production libraries is a stronger, more honest demonstration of the underlying idea than any single source it cites.
justification: Independent verification, not trust in the article's printed output. (1) Core bug: I wrote my own standalone program (not copied) that clones {int.MinValue, 1}, sorts it with Array.Sort(copy, (a,b) => a - b), and confirmed the result is [1, -2147483648] — not sorted — while unchecked(int.MinValue - 1) really does equal int.MaxValue (2147483647), and confirmed Array.Sort(copy, (a,b) => a.CompareTo(b)) produces the correct [-2147483648, 1]. This reproduces the article's central claim exactly, from first principles, on .NET SDK 10.0.401. (2) Generator/shrinker: I wrote an independent reimplementation with a deliberately different generator (rng.Next(5)==0 edge injection vs. the article's rng.Next(4)==0, still full-range byte reinterpretation) and a deliberately different shrink strategy (linear halving toward zero instead of the article's binary search, same drop-one-element move). Across 50 independent seeds x 200 trials each, my reimplementation found the sortedness violation in 50/50 seeds, and for seed=2 it found trial 1 already fails and shrinks to the same minimal [-2147483648, 1] the article reports — strong independent confirmation the technique and the specific numbers are real, not fabricated. (3) CsCheck: I extracted the article's cscheck-demo block into a standalone script and ran it three times outside the harness; it reproduces the exact same minimal counterexample [-25, -1062590646, 1539332543] every time under the pinned seed '2fDh2sAGsnI3', while the shrink/skip counts genuinely vary run to run (78, 70, 69 skipped across my three runs) — exactly matching the article's own claim that CsCheck 'shrinks in parallel across threads' so those counts (and only those counts) are correctly wildcarded with [...] in the article's expected output. I independently confirmed CsCheck resolves to exactly 4.9.1 (checked the local NuGet cache at ~/.nuget/packages/cscheck, and confirmed 4.9.1 is the latest 4.x release on nuget.org), matching the article's stated version. I also confirmed -1062590646 - 1539332543 genuinely overflows int (exact value -2601923189, wraps unchecked to +1693044107, flipping the comparison's sign) and that FsCheck.Xunit and FsCheck.Xunit.v3 are both real, live NuGet packages. (4) Sources: fetched all six cited pages directly (not from memory) and confirmed every quoted fragment against the raw page text. Five of six quotes are exactly verbatim. One is not: the article attributes 'FsCheck automatically displays a minimal counter-example' (hyphenated) to fscheck.github.io/FsCheck/, but that page's own HTML (stripped and checked directly, not summarized) reads 'a minimal counter example' with no hyphen; the hyphenated spelling instead appears on the FsCheck GitHub README, which the article cites for a different quote in the same sentence. The words and the meaning are both correct — this is not a fabricated or reworded quote in the spirit of the brief's hard rule against invented content — but it is not letter-for-letter verbatim to the specific page it is attributed to, so it is reported as a real, if narrow, finding rather than waved through. I confirmed all six front-matter sources are cited inline in the body (none orphaned), confirmed every internal crosslink resolves (/algorithms/binary-search/#the-midpoint-that-overflows exists as a real heading anchor; /glossary/#unit-test and /glossary/#invariant both exist as real glossary entries with matching term slugs; the prerequisites/testing/unit-testing-fundamentals article exists), and confirmed no NEEDS_MARKUS or other placeholder markers remain. I checked the article's arithmetic claims by hand: the seven opening unit tests really do span exactly [-8, 842] (verified against every literal in the test bodies), '4.3 billion' and int's actual range, and '1.8 x 10^19 possible pairs of ints' (= 2^64, correct) all check out. The 'range about 1,700 wide' sentence is also arithmetically exact once read as the span of possible a-b results over [-8, 842] (max 842-(-8)=850, min -8-842=-850, span 1700) rather than the span of the values themselves (850) — correct, but the switch from 'value range' to 'difference range' isn't spelled out, which a careful reader computing 842-(-8)=850 by hand could find momentarily confusing; flagged as a minor clarity nit, not an error. I ran node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/testing/property-based-testing.md five times in a row from this worktree; all five passed identically (PASS testing/property-based-testing.md blocks=19 executed=7), confirming the determinism story: every text-output block in the article (proptest, permutation-check, fixed-check, median-preview, median-fix) is byte-exact with no wildcards because the hand-rolled generator is seeded with System.Random and a fixed seed, which is genuinely deterministic across .NET versions and runs; only the CsCheck block's shrink/skip counts are wildcarded, and that wildcarding is the correct, honest call given CsCheck's documented parallel shrinking, not a dodge. Restraint claims hold: grepped the full article body for 'FsCheck' and found zero code fences using it (only prose citations of its own README/docs, correctly quoted almost letter-for-letter), and grepped for 'QuickCheck' and found exactly one mention ('a newer, C#-first library inspired by QuickCheck'), sourced straight to CsCheck's own README with no invented history, dates or attribution beyond what that source actually says. This is a genuinely strong, rigorously self-checking round-1 draft: a real bug, independently reproduced three separate ways (by hand, by a differently-built reimplementation, and by a real production library), honest and correctly-scoped restraint, and near-perfect sourcing. The one narrow quote-spelling mismatch and one clarity nit keep it just under a 9.5, but neither touches the substance of any claim in the piece.

issues.location: "Beyond a toy: FsCheck and CsCheck" section: "When a property fails, \"FsCheck automatically displays a minimal counter-example\" ([FsCheck Documentation](https://fscheck.github.io/FsCheck/))"
issues.problem: The quoted text is attributed to fscheck.github.io/FsCheck/, but that page's own text (fetched and stripped of HTML directly to rule out a rendering artifact) reads 'a minimal counter example' with no hyphen. The hyphenated spelling 'counter-example' the article uses instead appears on the FsCheck GitHub README (github.com/fscheck/FsCheck), which is cited earlier in the same sentence for a different quote. The words and meaning are unchanged either way, so this is not a fabricated or reworded quote in the sense the editorial brief's hard rule targets, but it is not letter-for-letter verbatim to the specific page the parenthetical attributes it to.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either drop the hyphen to match fscheck.github.io/FsCheck/ exactly ('a minimal counter example'), or re-attribute the quote to the GitHub README (github.com/fscheck/FsCheck) where 'counter-example' is the actual spelling.

issues.location: "What those seven tests didn't check" section: "The seven tests sampled a range about 1,700 wide out of one roughly 4.3 billion wide"
issues.problem: This is arithmetically correct but not obviously so: the individual test values span -8 to 842 (850 wide, matching the sentence right before it), while 1,700 is the span of possible a - b results over that domain (842 - (-8) = 850 at one extreme, -8 - 842 = -850 at the other, a spread of 1,700). A reader who just computed 842 - (-8) = 850 by hand, as the preceding sentence invites, could be momentarily thrown by '1,700' with no bridging clause.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add a short clause making the switch explicit, e.g. "...a range about 1,700 wide (the spread of every a - b the comparer could see, from -850 to 850) out of one roughly 4.3 billion wide..."
